title: The "God Struct" (Mega-Context)
pattern: A single giant struct containing references or instances of almost every repository, client, config, and utility service in the entire application, serving as an omniscient intermediary.
why_bad: Extremely tight coupling and heavy borrow-checker friction. Passing the entire `SystemEngine` around (or taking `&mut self` on it) locks down the entire application's resources, preventing concurrent operations or parallel processing of distinct sub-components. It violates the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) and obscures what individual sub-tasks actually depend on.
detection: Look for structs containing more than 7-10 independent service handles, database connections, or clients, coupled with methods that only use a small subset of those handles.
counterexample: The root application coordinator or compose root during startup, which exists purely to instantiate and link independent services before entering the execution loop.
fix: Decompose the giant struct into smaller, focused service blocks and pass only the specific, required sub-dependencies directly to functions.
source: *Martin Fowler - Refactoring (1999)*, Chapter 3, "Large Class"; *Steve McConnell - Code Complete (2004)*, Chapter 6, "Working Classes" (Riel's heuristic of critical data members); *Robert C. Martin - Clean Architecture (2017)*, Chapter 7, "SRP".
